title: Basic Analogies
source: MindSpark Grade 5 Aptitude & Reasoning | Chapter 6: Basic Analogies
learningGoals: Identify the relationship between the first word pair and apply it to find the missing word.
Solve part-to-whole analogies by recognising that the first word is a part of the second word.
Solve material-object analogies by identifying what material is used to make which object.
Solve action analogies by matching a person or animal to their characteristic action.
coreIdeas: In any analogy A:B :: C:D, the relationship between A and B is exactly the same as the relationship between C and D.
Always state the relationship in a sentence first: 'A is the __ of B' — then apply the same sentence to C to find D.
Common relationship types: sound (animal → sound), habitat (animal → home), young (animal → baby), tool (job → tool), material (raw material → object), part-whole.
If two answers seem possible, pick the one where the relationship is most precise and specific.

workedExamples.solution: Relationship: A lion's sound is a roar. A dog's sound is a bark. Answer: Bark.
workedExamples.concept: Word:Word analogy — animal to its characteristic sound

workedExamples.solution: Relationship: A wheel is a part of a car. A page is a part of a book. Answer: Book.
workedExamples.concept: Part-to-whole analogy — the first word is a component of the second

workedExamples.solution: Relationship: A shirt is made from cotton. Shoes (or a belt or a bag) are made from leather. Most common answer: Shoes.
workedExamples.concept: Material-object analogy — raw material to the object made from it

onboarding.coachIntro: Spark introduces analogies with a relatable example ('Pen is to writing as fork is to eating — they both serve a purpose!'). Opens with a simple word:word analogy.
onboarding.placementRule: Start at Group A. If the learner cannot articulate the relationship, provide the sentence frame 'A is the __ of B' and practice two examples before continuing.

mission.missionPromise: By the end you will solve any word analogy in seconds by always finding the relationship first — a skill that boosts vocabulary, logic, and reading comprehension!
mission.successCelebration: Show an 'Analogy Solved!' badge after each group. At lesson end, award the 'Analogy Ace' trophy.

microLessonPattern: Coach names the analogy type and gives a real-life hook example.
Coach works a full example on the board, stating the relationship in a sentence.
Coach reads the practice question aloud.
Student states the relationship and then gives the answer.
Instant feedback celebrates correct relationships and answers.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: Award 10–20 XP per group, increasing through the lesson.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Show streak flame; one free retry before streak breaks.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each group unlocks an analogy-themed badge.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Coach praise + XP burst + progress rail tick after every correct answer.

reviewLoop.trigger: Two incorrect attempts trigger a mini-reteach showing the relationship-sentence method.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Offer the completed relationship sentence and ask only for the missing word.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance after correct answer plus completed tryPrompt.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Groups with two errors return as review cards next session.

beats.teacherLine: Hello, language detective! An analogy is a connection between two pairs of words where the same relationship links both pairs. Here is an example: pen is to writing as fork is to eating — the relationship is 'tool used for the action'. Today we will practise four types of analogies: word-to-word (sounds, habitats, babies), part-to-whole, material-to-object, and action analogies. The golden rule for ALL analogies: always find the relationship first, then apply it!
beats.boardAction: Write 'Analogies — A:B :: C:D'. Explain: 'The relationship between A and B is the SAME as between C and D.' List 4 types: (1) Word:Word (sound/home/young), (2) Part:Whole, (3) Material:Object, (4) Action analogy.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Quick warm-up: Cat : Kitten :: Dog : ? (Hint: kitten is a baby cat — what is a baby dog?)
beats.fallbackHint: The relationship is 'animal : its young (baby)'. A baby cat is called a kitten. A baby dog is called a puppy.

svgAnimation.text: Golden rule: find the relationship, then apply it

beats.teacherLine: Let me demonstrate the relationship-first method! Question: Cow : Milk :: Hen : ? Step 1 — state the relationship: 'A cow gives milk.' Step 2 — apply it: 'A hen gives ___.' The answer is eggs! One more: Pen : Ink :: Brush : ? Relationship: 'A pen uses ink.' Apply: 'A brush uses ___.' Answer: Paint! Always say the relationship out loud — it makes the answer obvious almost every time!
beats.boardAction: Write 'Cow:Milk :: Hen:?' with relationship: 'A cow gives milk → a hen gives EGGS'. Write 'Pen:Ink :: Brush:?' with relationship: 'A pen uses ink → a brush uses PAINT'. Circle the answers.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Try this one: Carpenter : Wood :: Potter : ? State the relationship first!
beats.expectedStudentResponse: Clay — a carpenter works with wood, a potter works with clay.
beats.fallbackHint: The relationship is 'person : the material they work with'. A carpenter works with wood. What does a potter work with? Clay — potters shape clay to make pots.

svgAnimation.text: Relationship: A cow gives milk → A hen gives EGGS
Relationship: A pen uses ink → A brush uses PAINT

beats.teacherLine: Excellent! Your analogy toolkit is ready. Step 1: read the given pair. Step 2: state the relationship in a sentence. Step 3: apply that same relationship to the second pair to find the missing word. When two answers seem possible, pick the most specific, direct relationship. Work through Groups A to F — state the relationship for every question!
beats.boardAction: Show analogy framework: 'A is the [relationship] of B. Therefore, C is the [relationship] of ___.' List common relationships: sound (roar/bark/moo), young (kitten/puppy/calf), home (kennel/nest/den), material (cotton/leather/wood), part-whole, action.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Before the groups — what is the relationship in: Fish : Scales :: Bird : ?
beats.expectedStudentResponse: Feathers — a fish is covered in scales, a bird is covered in feathers.
beats.fallbackHint: The relationship is 'animal : its body covering'. A fish has scales. A bird has feathers.

svgAnimation.text: Frame: A is the [R] of B → C is the [R] of ?
Sound | Young | Home | Material | Part-Whole | Action
Tip: always say the relationship out loud first!

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's crack this code! Animals have their own languages — lions roar, cows moo, frogs croak. Let's turn these facts into analogy superpowers!

boardDemo.title: Animal Sound Analogies
steps: Lion : Roar → a lion makes the sound roar
Apply: Duck : ? → a duck makes the sound quack
More pairs: Cat:Meow, Cow:Moo, Frog:Croak, Bee:Buzz
Relationship sentence: 'An X makes the sound ___'
boardDemo.teacherLine: Say the relationship out loud: 'A lion makes the sound roar.' Now say: 'A dog makes the sound ___.' The answer pops right out — bark! This sentence method works every time.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Lion : Roar :: Cat : ? (What sound does a cat make?)
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! A bee makes a buzz, and a frog makes a croak. Relationship: animal : its sound. Brilliant!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: say it out loud — 'A bee buzzes, so a frog ___.' A frog makes the sound croak.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's crack this code! Every animal has a home with a special name — a dog has a kennel, a bee has a hive. Knowing these is key for analogy questions!

boardDemo.title: Animal Home Analogies
steps: Dog : Kennel → a dog lives in a kennel
Bee : Hive → a bee lives in a hive
Bird : Nest, Lion : Den, Horse : Stable, Rabbit : Burrow
Apply: Dog : Kennel :: Bird : ? → Nest
boardDemo.teacherLine: The relationship is 'animal : its home/dwelling'. Memorise common pairs: Dog-Kennel, Bird-Nest, Bee-Hive, Lion-Den, Horse-Stable, Rabbit-Burrow, Fish-Aquarium.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Dog : Kennel :: Bird : ? (Where does a bird live?)
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Excellent! A bee lives in a hive, and a horse lives in a stable. Relationship: animal : its home. Perfect!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: a bee's home is a hive. A horse's home is a stable (that big building where horses are kept on farms).

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's crack this code! A wheel is part of a car. A page is part of a book. In part-to-whole analogies, the first word is always a piece or component of the second word!

boardDemo.title: Part-to-Whole Analogies
steps: Wheel : Car → a wheel is a part of a car
Apply: Page : ? → a page is a part of a BOOK
More: Key : Keyboard, Petal : Flower, Branch : Tree, Spoke : Wheel
Relationship: 'A is a part/component of B'
boardDemo.teacherLine: Ask yourself: is the first word a piece of something? If yes, it is a part-to-whole analogy. Find what larger thing the second pair's first word is a part of!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Wheel : Car :: Petal : ? (A petal is a part of which larger thing?)
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Spot on! A key is a part of a keyboard, and a spoke is a part of a wheel. Part-to-whole identified perfectly!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: a key is part of a keyboard. A spoke is that thin rod that goes from the centre of a wheel to the rim — so a spoke is part of a wheel.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's crack this code! Cotton makes shirts, leather makes shoes, wood makes furniture. Material-to-object analogies test whether you know what things are made from!

boardDemo.title: Material-to-Object Analogies
steps: Cotton : Shirt → cotton is the material used to make a shirt
Apply: Leather : ? → leather is used to make SHOES (or belt, bag)
More pairs: Wood:Furniture, Gold:Jewellery, Clay:Pot, Glass:Window, Wool:Sweater
Relationship: 'A is the raw material used to make B'
boardDemo.teacherLine: State the relationship: 'Cotton is used to make shirts.' Then apply: 'Leather is used to make ___.' Shoes, belts, and bags are all made of leather — pick the most common exam answer: Shoes.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Cotton : Shirt :: Leather : ? (What is leather commonly used to make?)
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Brilliant! Wood is used to make furniture, and gold is used to make jewellery. Material-to-object relationship perfectly identified!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: what shiny objects do people wear that are made of gold? Rings, necklaces, bangles — all types of jewellery. Gold : Jewellery.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Action analogies — person or animal to action
sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's crack this code! Doctors treat patients, teachers teach students, birds fly — action analogies link a person or animal to what they characteristically do!

boardDemo.title: Action Analogies
steps: Doctor : Treats :: Teacher : ? → a doctor treats (patients), a teacher TEACHES (students)
Bird : Flies :: Fish : ? → a bird flies, a fish SWIMS
Soldier : Fights :: Farmer : ? → a soldier fights, a farmer GROWS (crops)/FARMS
Relationship: 'A characteristically does action B'
boardDemo.teacherLine: The relationship is 'X : their main action'. Say: 'A doctor treats. A teacher ___.' The most direct, specific action is the answer. Avoid vague words — be precise!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Doctor : Treats :: Teacher : ? (What does a teacher do?)
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! A bird flies, and a fish swims. Both actions are how these animals move through their environment. Excellent analogy!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: a bird moves through air by flying. A fish moves through water by swimming. Bird:Flies :: Fish:Swims.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise F: Speed Round — Mixed Analogies
sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's crack this code — at speed! Four analogy types, three quick questions. State the type and answer fast!

boardDemo.title: Speed Round — All Analogy Types
steps: Word:Word — name the relationship (sound, young, home, body covering)
Part:Whole — first word is a piece of the second
Material:Object — first word is used to make the second
Action — first word characteristically performs the action
boardDemo.teacherLine: For every question: say the type, say the relationship sentence, then give the answer. This takes 10 seconds and is always correct!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Ready? Three quick analogy questions — name the type and answer!
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Q1: Lion : Roar :: Frog : ? | Q2: Petal : Flower :: Key : ? | Q3: Wool : Sweater :: Clay : ?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: AMAZING! Q1: sound analogy — frog croaks. Q2: part-to-whole — key is part of keyboard. Q3: material-object — clay is used to make a pot. Full marks — Analogy Ace!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Q1 — lion's sound is roar, frog's sound is croak. Q2 — petal is part of flower, key is part of keyboard. Q3 — wool makes a sweater, clay makes a pot.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Final challenge: create your own analogy for each type — Word:Word, Part:Whole, Material:Object, and Action. Share all four!
